source_title: Unmanned Aerial Vehicles; Search Warrant; Exceptions
citation: IC 35-33-5-9 (as added by P.L.170-2014, SEC.19; amended by P.L.57-2016, SEC.2; P.L.136-2019, SEC.1)
uas_topic: Law-enforcement UAV use restriction; private-property search/surveillance warrant requirement
regulated_activity: Using an unmanned aerial vehicle on or over private property, or to conduct a search, perform surveillance, or obtain a photograph or video of private property or of individuals, items, or structures on private property
requirement_type: Search-warrant requirement, with an exception where a warrant would not be required for the same search if conducted without a UAV
summary: IC 35-33-5-9 requires a law enforcement officer to obtain a search warrant to use an unmanned aerial vehicle (1) on or over private property, or (2) to search, surveil, photograph, or video private property or persons/items/structures on private property, without the affected owner's consent. A warrant is not required if one would not be required for the same search conducted without a UAV. The statute does not itself regulate private/commercial UAS operators.

requirement_type: Prohibition (Class A misdemeanor; Level 6 felony if a prior unrelated conviction, or if the images/recordings are published, posted online, or transmitted to another person)
summary: IC 35-45-4-5(g) makes it remote aerial voyeurism for a person, with intent to peep, to operate a UAV so that it enters the airspace above or surrounding another person's occupied dwelling to capture images, photographs, video, or audio of that person while inside the dwelling or on adjoining land not visible from a public area, without consent. Subsection (h) elevates the offense to a Level 6 felony for a repeat offense or if the material is published, posted online, or transmitted to another person. This is a subsection within Indiana's broader voyeurism statute (Sec. 5), distinct from the separate remote aerial harassment offense at IC 35-45-10-6 (IN-003).

source_title: Trafficking With an Inmate; Carrying Contraband Into a Correctional Facility / Trafficking With an Inmate Outside a Facility (UAV-delivered contraband)
citation: IC 35-44.1-3-5 and IC 35-44.1-3-6 (both amended by P.L.22-2024, part of Senate Enrolled Act 182, signed 2024-03-11)
regulated_activity: Delivering, carrying, or receiving contraband or another article to or from an inmate of a penal/juvenile facility, or delivering/placing contraband for an inmate being transported outside a facility, including by means of an unmanned aerial vehicle, without the facility head's prior authorization
requirement_type: Prohibition (Class A misdemeanor; Level 5 felony if the article is a controlled substance, chemical intoxicant, deadly weapon, or wireless device; Level 6 or Level 5 felony under Sec. 6 depending on contraband type)
permit_or_approval_required: N/A (facility head's prior authorization is the only avoidance mechanism)
summary: IC 35-44.1-3-5 makes it trafficking with an inmate, a Class A misdemeanor (Level 5 felony for certain contraband), to deliver, carry, or receive an article to or from an inmate or juvenile-facility resident without the facility head's prior authorization, expressly including delivery, carrying, or receipt 'through the use of an unmanned aerial vehicle.' IC 35-44.1-3-6 creates a parallel offense, trafficking with an inmate outside a facility, for delivering or placing contraband where an inmate being transported outside a facility could obtain it, likewise expressly including delivery or placement by UAV. Both sections were amended in 2024 (P.L.22-2024) as part of Senate Enrolled Act 182, enacted after the Indiana Department of Correction reported more than 30 drone sightings and over a dozen confirmed drone-delivered contraband drops at state correctional facilities in 2023.

source_title: Use of Unmanned Aerial Vehicles to Aid Hunting
uas_topic: UAV-aided-hunting restriction (wildlife/hunting), with agricultural-monitoring and post-harvest-recovery exceptions
regulated_party: Hunters and the general public (exceptions for DNR and its designees, government agents, educational/research institutions, veterinary care, and agricultural/nuisance-animal monitoring)
regulated_activity: Using a UAV to search for, scout, locate, or detect a wild animal to which a hunting season applies, as an aid to taking that animal, during the period beginning 14 days before the season and running through its last legal hunting hour
requirement_type: Prohibition during the defined season window; UAV-aided recovery of an already-legally-taken animal (including with infrared) is expressly permitted, but does not authorize entering another's property without permission
summary: IC 14-22-6-16(c) prohibits knowingly using a UAV to search for, scout, locate, or detect a wild animal covered by a hunting season, as an aid to taking it, during a window beginning 14 days before that season and ending at the close of legal hunting hours on the season's last day. Subsection (d) permits using a UAV with infrared capability to locate and recover an already-legally-taken animal, but does not authorize entering another person's property without the landowner's permission. Subsection (a) exempts the department and its designees, government-agency employees/agents performing official duties, educational/research institution personnel for bona fide purposes, UAV use to assist or provide veterinary care to a specific wild animal, and UAV use to monitor agricultural production or nuisance wild animals.

summary: New IC Article 10-22, added by Senate Bill 227 (2026 Reg. Sess.), designates the Indiana State Police as the statewide coordinating agency for counter-UAS activities authorized under federal law. It authorizes the state police to seek federal authorization to acquire, deploy, and operate counter-UAS systems; to designate local law-enforcement 'participating agencies' meeting federal training/readiness requirements; to designate Indianapolis as a pilot-project location given its concentration of high-risk sites; and to designate 'high-risk sites' including critical infrastructure, correctional facilities, airports, and large public/special-event-rated events. Counter-UAS systems must appear on the federal C-UAS Technology List. By its own terms (Chapter 1), the article applies only once a federal law authorizing state/local detection, tracking, identification, or mitigation of UAS is enacted and the Governor has published notice of that authorization in the Indiana Register; mitigation activity is barred absent express federal authorization.
